question: The clone drifts off the teacher's path and cannot get back. Can 8 examples of the teacher recovering from a small nudge teach it to recover?
measure: Successes out of 15 closed-loop tries (5 cube start positions, 3 repeats each), and safety counts per try: clipped frames (a command cut at a joint limit), limited frames (a command cut by the speed limiter) and unsafe-contact frames.
outcome: No. It still memorized the data, then failed all 15 tries, and it became unsafe: 291 clipped frames and 13 unsafe-contact frames per try from the normal start. The old clone had zero.
setup: A policy is the network that drives the arm. The teacher is a script that cheats by reading the cube's true position. The clone is a small network trained to copy one 450-step recording of the teacher (experiment 02). It matched the recording almost exactly and still failed 3/3, because its small errors pile up (covariate shift). A recovery example is one extra training row: push the arm slightly off course, let the simulator settle, and record what the teacher commands from there. "ACT units" are the motor-range units the commands are stored in. The memorization bar is the offline gate from experiment 02: mean squared error at most 1e-6 and largest error at most 0.01 ACT on the 450 normal rows. A handoff test starts the clone exactly at one of the recovery states and asks whether it can finish from there.

parts.title: Do 8 recovery rows fix closed-loop control?
parts.why: If a few labelled recoveries teach correction, the clone should pass. If not, sparse examples are not enough.
parts.did: Injected one 0.01-ACT perturbation just before each of 8 phases: approach (70), first contact (195), seating (205), closure (255), lift (315), transport (365), placement (386) and release (419). Added those 8 rows to the 450. Same network, inputs, seed and schedule. Then ran the standard 15 rollouts.
parts.conclusion: The 458-row clone passed the offline bar and then failed all 15 standard rollouts. The four starts with the cube moved 1.5 mm were worse: 359-450 clipped frames per repeat and up to 32 limited frames.

parts.title: Does it at least recover from the exact states it was trained on?
parts.why: Maybe it knows the recoveries but never reaches those states. Starting it exactly there removes that excuse.
parts.did: Handed control to each clone at each of the 8 recovery states and let it finish the episode.

cells: release only; clipped after every failed handoff

parts.conclusion: The recovery rows made the clone worse at the very states they covered. Eight isolated points next to a continuous path force the network to bend sharply between them, and those bends come out as huge commands.

trust.text: Only the 8 rows changed: same architecture, inputs, optimizer, seed, 30k schedule, normalization and safety path.
Each recovery state was captured twice with identical results, and the teacher finished the task from each with zero safety events.

These runs used MuJoCo 3.11.0 by accident (a stray pip install; the project pins 3.9.0). The reports were moved to a quarantine folder and the training was not re-run. The log says the conclusion did not depend on the exact counts.
The log says the nudge was "half a degree". The source gives 0.01 ACT units, not degrees.
The log gives the lift as 5 mm; the source is 0.005173 m. One seed. Simulation only.

meaning: Near-exact fit on the recording is not a safe promotion test, even with some recovery coverage added. The next question was whether the 8 rows were simply weighted too heavily (experiment 04).
lesson: A handful of recovery examples does not teach recovery, and it can break what already worked. The offline memorization bar could not see any of it.

next.title: Turn down the weight of the recovery rows (experiment 04)
next.why: Maybe a lighter touch keeps the normal start safe.

next.title: Corrections from the clone's own states, as full trajectories (experiment 06)

log:
**TL;DR:** I added 8 examples of the script recovering from small mistakes, and
the clone got worse: it failed all 15 tries and started slamming into its joint
limits.

**Problem.** The clone from entry 02 drifts off the script's path and has no
idea how to get back.

*How we know:* it failed 3/3, its joints were half a degree off by step 74, and
the same commands replayed on the script's states worked fine. I didn't know if
showing it a few recoveries would be enough.

**Experiment.** At 8 points across the task (approach, contact, closure, lift,
carry, place, release and so on), nudge the arm half a degree off course, record
what the script does from there, and add those 8 rows to the 450 training rows.
Same model, same training.

*What we hope to learn:* if a few labeled recoveries teach correction, the clone
should pass. If not, sparse examples aren't enough.

**Outcome.** It still hit the memorization bar, then failed 0/15 (5 cube
positions, 3 tries each), every try killed by safety violations:

- On the normal start, 291 commands per try got clipped at the joint limits,
  and it lifted the cube 5 mm.
- Even when I started it exactly at the recovery states it was trained on, it
  only finished 1 of 8 (the old clone finished 3).

Eight points is nothing next to a continuous path. To fit them, the network
bends hard between them, and those bends become huge commands. Like teaching
someone to drive with 8 photos of near-crashes.

*Note:* these numbers came from the wrong MuJoCo version (entry 09) and were
never re-run; the conclusion didn't depend on the exact counts.

**Takeaway:** a handful of recovery examples doesn't teach recovery, and it can
break what already worked. The memorization bar couldn't see any of it.
